concepts.name: Lazy<T> thread-safety modes and exception caching
App Service deployment slot swaps and slot settings

questions.prompt: A singleton holds `new Lazy<VaultConfig>(() => LoadFromVault())`. The vault is down for a moment at startup, so the first `.Value` throws. What does the next `.Value` call do once the vault is back?

choices.text: It runs `LoadFromVault()` again and returns the config, as failures aren't stored
It throws the same exception again, because the factory's exception is cached
It returns `null`, because the failed initialization left the value unset for good
It blocks until the first thread's factory call is retried and completes successfully

questions.explanation: `Lazy<T>` with a value factory and the default mode (`ExecutionAndPublication`) caches exceptions: the factory is never run again, and every later `.Value` rethrows the same exception. So a transient startup failure becomes permanent for that instance. `LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly` doesn't cache exceptions, but lets several threads run the factory at once.

sources.title: Lazy Initialization - .NET Framework
sources.claim: Lazy<T> is thread-safe (ExecutionAndPublication) by default; with a valueFactory, exception caching is on, so a factory exception is rethrown on every later Value access and the factory is never re-invoked; with PublicationOnly several threads may race to run the factory, the first result wins, and exceptions are not cached.

questions.prompt: A .NET API container has `requests.cpu: 250m`, `limits.cpu: 500m` and `limits.memory: 512Mi`. In a traffic spike it tries to use 2 CPUs and 700Mi. What does Kubernetes do?

choices.text: Kills it for going over its CPU limit, and caps its memory at 512Mi
Lets it burst past both limits, as only requests apply at runtime
Moves the pod to a bigger node, since requests are rechecked live
Throttles it at 500m CPU, and may OOM-kill it once it's over 512Mi

questions.explanation: Requests are for scheduling: they decide which node can hold the pod. Limits apply at runtime, differently per resource: the CPU limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces by throttling, so the API slows down, while going over the memory limit can get the container terminated (OOM-killed) when the kernel sees memory pressure. Kubernetes never moves a running pod because it is busy.

sources.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers
sources.claim: The scheduler uses requests to choose a node; a CPU limit is a hard limit enforced by kernel throttling; a container over its memory limit may be terminated by the kernel when it detects memory pressure, so memory limits are enforced reactively; a limit with no request is copied as the request.

questions.prompt: You deploy a .NET API to an App Service staging slot and swap it into production. Explain what the swap does to avoid downtime, which settings move with the app and which stay, and how you would roll back.

model_answer.summary: The swap prepares and warms the staging instances with production's settings before switching routing, moves unmarked app settings with the app, and is rolled back by swapping again.
key_points: Before switching, App Service applies the production slot's slot-specific settings to the staging instances, restarts them and warms each one up with an HTTP request
Only when every instance is warm does it switch routing, so production stays online and no requests are dropped
App settings and connection strings swap with the app unless marked as deployment slot settings; custom domains, scale settings and managed identities stay with the slot
To roll back, swap the same two slots again to bring back the last known good app

questions.explanation: All the preparation happens on the source slot while the target keeps serving. The common mistake is assuming connection strings stay put: an unmarked staging connection string follows the app into production.

sources.title: Set Up Staging Environments - Azure App Service
sources.claim: A swap first applies the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot's instances, restarts and warms them up, and only then switches routing, so the target stays online; app settings and connection strings swap unless marked as deployment slot settings, while custom domains, scale settings and managed identities stay; swapping the same slots again rolls back.

choices.text: Several threads may run the factory; the first result wins, and errors aren't cached
Only one thread runs the factory, and its exception is cached for every later caller
Each thread runs the factory once and keeps its own value, much like a `ThreadLocal<T>`
One thread runs the factory, and other threads see `null` until it is published

questions.explanation: With `PublicationOnly` threads race to initialize: each may run the factory, one result is published and every thread gets it. Exceptions aren't cached, so a later `.Value` can succeed. Running the factory once and caching its exception is the default `ExecutionAndPublication` behaviour; per-thread values are `ThreadLocal<T>`.

questions.prompt: Explain how Kubernetes uses a container's resource requests and limits for CPU and memory, and what each choice means for a latency-sensitive .NET API.

model_answer.summary: Requests place the pod; a CPU limit throttles and so adds latency, while a memory limit ends in the container being killed.
key_points: The scheduler uses requests to choose a node with enough unreserved capacity
A CPU limit is a hard limit enforced by the kernel through throttling: the app slows down but keeps running
Going over the memory limit can get the container terminated (OOM-killed), enforced reactively when the kernel sees memory pressure
If you set a limit but no request, Kubernetes copies the limit as the request

questions.explanation: CPU and memory fail differently at their limits: CPU throttling shows up as tail latency, a memory overrun as restarts. Requests set too low pack too many pods onto a node; limits set too low throttle or kill a healthy app.

sources.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers
sources.claim: The scheduler uses requests to choose a node; a CPU limit is a hard limit enforced by kernel throttling; a container over its memory limit may be terminated by the kernel when it detects memory pressure, so memory limits are enforced reactively; a limit with no request is copied as the request.

questions.prompt: Production and staging both have an app setting `ConnectionStrings__Db`, and staging's points at the staging database. Nobody marked it as a deployment slot setting. What happens after you swap staging into production?

choices.text: Production keeps its own value, because connection settings always stay with the slot
The swap is refused, because both slots define the same setting with different values
Production uses the staging database, because unmarked settings swap with the app
Both slots end up on the production database, as the target's values are copied over

questions.explanation: App settings and connection strings follow the app across a swap unless you tick "Deployment slot setting" (or pass `--slot-settings`), which makes them stay with their slot. Only slot-specific settings from the target are applied to the source before the switch. Mark environment-specific values as slot settings before the first swap.

sources.title: Set Up Staging Environments - Azure App Service
sources.claim: A swap first applies the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot's instances, restarts and warms them up, and only then switches routing, so the target stays online; app settings and connection strings swap unless marked as deployment slot settings, while custom domains, scale settings and managed identities stay; swapping the same slots again rolls back.

questions.prompt: You deploy a .NET API to an App Service staging slot and swap it into production. Which statements about the swap are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Staging gets production's slot settings and warms up before routing switches
An unmarked connection string in staging moves into production with the app
To roll back, you swap the same two slots again
Custom domain names and scale settings move with the app to the other slot
Production goes offline briefly while the routing rules are switched over

questions.explanation: A swap first applies the target slot's slot-specific settings to every source instance, restarts and warms them up, and only then switches routing, so production stays online and no requests are dropped. App settings and connection strings swap with the app unless marked as deployment slot settings, so an unmarked staging connection string follows the app into production. Custom domains and scale settings aren't swapped: they stay with the slot. Swapping the same slots again brings back the last known good app.

sources.title: Set Up Staging Environments - Azure App Service
sources.claim: A swap applies the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot's instances, restarts and warms them up, then switches routing, so the target stays online; app settings and connection strings swap unless marked as slot settings, while custom domain names and scale settings aren't swapped; swapping the same two slots again rolls back.

questions.prompt: You set CPU and memory requests and limits on the container of a latency-sensitive .NET API in Kubernetes. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The scheduler uses the requests to pick a node with enough capacity
At its CPU limit the container is throttled, which shows up as latency
Going over the memory limit can get the container OOM-killed
At its CPU limit the container is killed and restarted by the kernel
A container never uses more memory than its request, even on an idle node

questions.explanation: The scheduler places a pod using its requests. A CPU limit is a hard limit enforced by throttling: the app keeps running but slows, which a latency-sensitive API feels as tail latency. A memory limit is enforced reactively: a container over it may be OOM-killed when the kernel sees memory pressure. CPU over the limit is throttled, not killed, and a container may use more than its request when the node has spare capacity, up to its limit.

sources.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers
sources.claim: The scheduler uses requests to choose a node; a CPU limit is a hard limit enforced by kernel throttling; a container over its memory limit may be terminated by the kernel when it detects memory pressure; a container may use more than its request when the node has the resource available.
